p: In Australia, Christmas is in summer. We go to the beach and have a big lunch. Then we play cricket with my cousins.
On New Year's Eve we stayed up late. At midnight we watched fireworks over the harbour. Everyone cheered and hugged.
My family celebrates Chuseok. We make half moon rice cakes together. Then we bow to Grandma and Grandpa.
At Easter we had an egg hunt in the backyard. I found eggs under the bushes. My little sister found the most.
On Harmony Day we wore orange. We shared food from our families. I tried curry, sushi and baklava.
For my birthday we had a party at the park. We played games and ate cake. My friends sang happy birthday to me.

p: Christmas in Australia is very different from Christmas in snowy countries. Because it is summer, many families have a barbecue, eat seafood and cold salads, and go to the beach or the pool. Some people still decorate with snowflakes and eat hot roast dinners, even when it is thirty-five degrees outside.

Chuseok is one of the most important holidays in Korea. It happens in autumn and celebrates the harvest. Families travel to their hometowns, prepare special foods such as songpyeon and pay respect to their ancestors. In Australia, Korean families often gather to share food and play traditional games.

NAIDOC Week is held every July to celebrate the history, culture and achievements of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Schools and communities hold events such as art displays, storytelling, dance performances and flag-raising ceremonies. It is a great time for everyone to learn more about the world's oldest continuing cultures.

Lunar New Year is celebrated by many Asian communities around the world. People clean their houses to sweep away bad luck, decorate with red and gold, and share big family meals. In Australian cities, parades feature lion dances, dragon dances and firecrackers. Each year is named after one of twelve animals.

Anzac Day is held on the twenty-fifth of April. It remembers Australians and New Zealanders who have served in wars and peacekeeping missions. Many people go to dawn services and marches, and some cook Anzac biscuits. A minute's silence is held to show respect for those who died.

Every year our school holds a fete. Parents run stalls selling cakes, plants and second-hand books. There are rides, face painting and a dunk tank where students can soak a teacher. The money raised helps buy new resources for the school.

p: Festivals play an important role in community life. They bring people together to celebrate shared values, mark the changing seasons or remember significant events. In multicultural Australia, festivals also provide opportunities for communities to share their traditions with others. Food stalls, music, dance and craft activities allow visitors to experience cultures that may be unfamiliar to them.

The date of Australia Day has become the subject of national debate. The twenty-sixth of January marks the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788, which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people describe as Invasion Day or Survival Day. Some argue the national day should be moved to a date that all Australians can celebrate, while others believe it should remain unchanged.

The Garma Festival, held each year in north-east Arnhem Land, is one of Australia's most significant Indigenous cultural events. Hosted by the Yolngu people, it features traditional dance, music, art and ceremony. It also brings together political leaders, researchers and community members to discuss issues such as education, health and land rights. Visitors are invited to learn directly from Yolngu elders.

Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. During this month, many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset, avoiding food and drink. The fast is broken each evening with a meal called iftar, often shared with family and friends. Ramadan is a time for prayer, reflection and charity, and it ends with the joyful celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

Agricultural shows have been part of Australian life since the nineteenth century. Originally, they allowed farmers to compete for prizes, exchange ideas and display their best animals and produce. Today, shows in cities and country towns still feature livestock judging and baking competitions, alongside rides, fireworks and showbags. They remain an important link between city and country communities.

Light festivals have become popular in many cities. Vivid Sydney, for example, projects colourful animations onto buildings such as the Opera House and hosts concerts and talks. These events attract large crowds during the colder months and support local restaurants and businesses. However, organisers must also consider crowd safety, transport and the environmental impact of large-scale events.

p: National days are intended to unify citizens around shared values, yet they can also expose deep divisions. In Australia, the twenty-sixth of January commemorates the arrival of British ships in 1788, an event that marked the beginning of dispossession for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Annual protests and alternative events have prompted some councils to change how they mark the day. The debate raises fundamental questions about whose history a nation chooses to celebrate.

Festivals have become an increasingly important part of the cultural and economic life of Australian cities. Events such as the Adelaide Fringe, Melbourne International Comedy Festival and Vivid Sydney attract hundreds of thousands of visitors, supporting hospitality, transport and creative industries. Governments often justify public funding by pointing to these economic returns. Critics, however, argue that the value of the arts should not be measured solely in dollars, emphasising their role in reflection, critique and community connection.

For migrant communities, maintaining festival traditions can be a powerful way of preserving identity. Yet traditions inevitably change in a new context. A harvest festival celebrated in autumn may fall in spring in Australia, and ingredients for traditional dishes may be difficult to find. Younger generations may participate differently from their parents. These adaptations illustrate that culture is not static but continually reinterpreted as communities negotiate belonging across different places.

Commemoration is never simply about the past; it reflects the concerns of the present. The way Anzac Day is observed has shifted over the past century, from a solemn occasion focused on grieving families, to a period of declining interest, to renewed popularity among young Australians. Historians have encouraged more inclusive remembrance, recognising the service of Aboriginal soldiers, women and others whose experiences were long overlooked.

Large festivals generate significant environmental impacts, including waste, energy use and transport emissions. Some organisers are responding with reusable cups, renewable power and incentives to use public transport. Sustainability is increasingly expected by audiences and sponsors alike. Yet achieving genuine reductions requires measuring impacts carefully and being transparent about results, rather than relying on symbolic gestures that may amount to little more than marketing.

Rituals and celebrations serve important psychological and social functions. They mark transitions such as birth, adulthood, marriage and death, providing structure during periods of change. Shared rituals can strengthen bonds and create a sense of continuity across generations. In increasingly diverse and secular societies, people often create new rituals or adapt old ones, demonstrating the enduring human need to gather, remember and find meaning together.
